market_context: United States/general English; FDA/USDA refrigeration guidance
title: How to organize your refrigerator to keep food safe longer

seo.title: How to organize your refrigerator for food safety
seo.meta_description: Keep ready-to-eat food above raw meat, raw poultry on the lowest level in leakproof containers, produce in drawers and the refrigerator at 40°F or below.
seo.search_intent: Arrange a refrigerator to reduce cross-contamination and maintain safe cold storage.

excerpt: Refrigerator organization is mainly about cold temperature and cross-contamination. Keep ready-to-eat and cooked foods above raw meat and poultry; store raw items low in leakproof containers; use produce drawers; and keep the refrigerator at 40°F or below. The door is warmer and better for less temperature-sensitive items.
content_html:
A tidy refrigerator is useful, but the real safety goal is to make it physically difficult for raw chicken juice to reach food that will be eaten without further cooking.

AreaBest use
Upper/middle shelvesCooked and ready-to-eat foods
Lowest shelfRaw meat, poultry and seafood in leakproof containers
Produce drawersFruits and vegetables
DoorLess temperature-sensitive condiments

The map works because it follows the direction of risk, not because the top shelf has special properties. Ready-to-eat foods are protected from raw foods; raw foods are contained and kept low; produce is organized according to humidity and use. If your refrigerator has specialized drawers or zones, adapt the layout without losing that logic.

Contain raw juices

Original meat packaging may leak. Put raw meat and poultry on a tray or in a container capable of catching liquid and keep it below ready-to-eat foods.

40°F is the important number

FDA recommends keeping the refrigerator at 40°F or below. An appliance thermometer gives more useful information than assuming a dial setting is accurate.

Do not pack so tightly that air cannot circulate

Cold air needs room to move. Overloading can create warmer pockets and make it harder for freshly stored leftovers to cool.

Use dates you can understand

Label leftovers and move older items forward. Refrigerator organization should reduce both foodborne risk and forgotten food waste.

Refrigerator shelves do not all run at exactly the same temperature, and the coldest spot is not identical in every appliance. A simple refrigerator thermometer is more useful than assuming a particular shelf is always coldest. What should remain constant is the separation of raw foods from foods that will be eaten without another cooking step.

Use closed, leak-resistant containers for raw meat and poultry even when they are on the bottom shelf. “Bottom shelf” is a second line of defense, not a substitute for containment. Ready-to-eat leftovers, cheese, washed produce and prepared foods belong above or otherwise protected from raw juices. This arrangement reduces the consequences of a torn package or unnoticed drip.

The door experiences larger temperature swings each time it is opened, so it is usually better suited to condiments and other products that tolerate variation. Highly perishable foods benefit from the more stable interior shelves. At the same time, avoid filling the refrigerator so tightly that cold air cannot circulate around containers.

Organization also has a time component. Date leftovers and place older items where you will see them instead of letting them migrate to the back. Keep foods that need to be used soon in a visible zone. A refrigerator can be at the correct temperature and still generate waste or safety mistakes if nobody knows how long a container has been there.

Produce drawers are mainly a humidity-management tool, not a universal safety barrier. Use them for fruits and vegetables according to the appliance design, but keep raw animal foods physically contained elsewhere. The best layout is the one that preserves the same principles even when the shelf geometry of your refrigerator is different.

A clean refrigerator layout also reduces cross-contamination during ordinary use. Store raw packages where you can remove them without dragging them over containers of leftovers, and clean any spill promptly instead of moving other foods through it. Do not rely on a refrigerator drawer labeled “meat” if liquid can escape from an unsealed package. For produce, keeping visibly dirty unwashed items separate from washed ready-to-eat produce can simplify meal preparation. The aim is not a perfect showroom arrangement; it is a repeatable system in which temperature-sensitive food stays cold, raw juices stay contained, dates remain visible and commonly used items are easy to reach without disturbing everything else.

Eggs and milk are best kept where the appliance maintains a stable cold temperature, not wherever the packaging happens to fit most conveniently. If your refrigerator manual identifies a dedicated cold zone, use it according to the manufacturer’s directions. The organizing principle remains the same: stable cold for perishables and physical barriers between raw and ready-to-eat foods.

The rule

Ready-to-eat food above, raw animal foods below, produce in drawers, and everything at 40°F or colder. Exact shelf temperatures vary by appliance, so containment and thermometer readings matter more than decorative zones.

faq.question: Where should raw chicken go in the fridge?
faq.answer: On the lowest practical shelf in a leakproof container, away from foods that will be eaten without cooking.
